issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around war-zone trauma appraisals of injustice/accountability and a threat pattern of hypervigilance, startle, and concentration problems. Self-harm to release overwhelming feelings introduces a distinct affect-regulation strategy that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and sits poorly with the formulation, where Maladaptive Strategies has only a modest reciprocal link with Threat and no links from Negative Appraisals. Given the rest of the profile, a more threat-management strategy would be expected; this item feels clinically out of pattern rather than impossible.

vignette:
Jamal, a 33-year-old African American man, had been back in the States for five years, but the dust of the war zone he'd served in as a relief worker still seemed to cling to his soul. The memory of the day the aid distribution point was attacked remained a raw, unaddressed wound. He had been there, trying to organize supplies, when the shelling started, followed by armed groups swarming the perimeter. He'd witnessed unspeakable acts, the targeting of civilians he was desperately trying to protect. He remembered the deafening cracks, the screams, the frantic scramble for cover, and his own desperate, futile attempts to shield a family huddled near a crumbling wall. The profound sense of helplessness, the sheer scale of the horror, had seared itself into him. What haunted him most was the lingering knowledge that the perpetrators had faced no consequences, a deep-seated injustice that still made his blood run cold. He had come to believe, with a crushing certainty, that he couldn't truly rely on himself when the stakes were highest, a conviction born from that day's overwhelming chaos.

In the years that followed, Jamal developed an elaborate internal architecture to manage the fallout. He found himself mentally detaching from the memories whenever fragments of the incident surfaced, as if watching a disturbing film of his own past rather than reliving it. He meticulously filled his days and evenings with distractions, anything to keep his mind from wandering back to that place. Yet, the world around him became a constant reminder of the threats he'd faced. Working as a social media manager, often in a bustling open-plan office, meant a continuous assault on his senses. Every new client meeting room or even a busy coffee shop became a tactical assessment; his eyes darted to exits, scanned faces, noting potential threats in the most innocuous movements. He was superalert, constantly watchful, on guard. A sudden car horn from the street below or a dropped coffee mug by a colleague would send a jolt through his body, his muscles tensing involuntarily, leaving him feeling jumpy and easily startled.

This heightened state of alert made his job increasingly difficult. He'd stare at his screen, tasked with crafting engaging content or analyzing campaign metrics, but the words would blur, his mind unable to string together a coherent thought for a brief. His concentration was shattered, his attention constantly pulled away by the peripheral hum of the office, the distant siren, or the unexpected vibration of his phone. The effort to appear functional, to keep his focus, was exhausting. He'd often miss critical details in client communications or overlook trending topics, consequences that accumulated over weeks and months, slowly eroding his professional confidence and his relationship with his team leader. The injustice of what he had witnessed, and the lack of accountability for those responsible, simmered beneath the surface, feeding a quiet rage that made sustained concentration on mundane tasks almost impossible.

At home, the quiet was often more terrifying than the noise. He'd find himself scanning his own living room, checking the locks multiple times, his hypervigilance extending even to the perceived safety of his own four walls. His wife, Maria, noticed his increasing withdrawal, his distant gaze, and the way he'd flinch at unexpected sounds. He had grown increasingly isolated, unable to articulate the persistent fear and the sense of profound unfairness that pervaded his every waking moment. The cumulative strain on his marriage, coupled with a recent performance review at work that highlighted his declining focus and engagement, finally propelled him to seek help. He was tired of living in a state of perpetual alert, tired of the gnawing conviction that he was fundamentally unreliable, and most of all, he was terrified that the man Maria married was disappearing, replaced by a ghost of the past he couldn't outrun. He longed for a sense of safety, a reprieve from the constant internal battle, and a way to reconcile with the unbearable truth of what he had endured.
